claims.claim: Borski says the third novella is told out of order with the reader left to piece the case together from a fragmentary narrative.
claims.source: Robert Borski, review of The Fifth Head of Cerberus, Ultan's Library, 28 August 2001
claims.quote: told anachronically, with the reader left to piece everything together

claims.claim: Wolfe told Science Fiction Studies that he writes a minimum of three passes over everything, an original plus at least two rewrites.
claims.source: Gene Wolfe, interviewed by Larry McCaffery, 'On Encompassing the Entire Universe', Science Fiction Studies #46, vol. 15 part 3, November 1988
claims.quote: an original and then at least two rewrites

claims.claim: Wolfe said some of his work goes through fifteen or more drafts.
claims.source: Gene Wolfe, interviewed by Larry McCaffery, Science Fiction Studies #46, November 1988
claims.quote: some of it goes 15 or even more drafts

claims.claim: Wolfe said he rewrote the opening pages of The Fifth Head of Cerberus at least eight or ten times.
claims.source: Gene Wolfe, interviewed by Larry McCaffery, Science Fiction Studies #46, November 1988
claims.quote: I completely rewrote those opening pages at least eight or ten times

claims.claim: Wolfe said the reason he rewrote that opening so many times was to establish the feeling of stagnation that governs what follows.
claims.source: Gene Wolfe, interviewed by Larry McCaffery, Science Fiction Studies #46, November 1988
claims.quote: the feeling of stagnation which affects a lot of

claims.claim: Wolfe said getting the language right matters most when he is trying to capture a specific atmosphere or cultural attitude in a story.
claims.source: Gene Wolfe, interviewed by Larry McCaffery, Science Fiction Studies #46, November 1988
claims.quote: trying to capture a specific atmosphere or cultural attitude in a story

claims.claim: Wolfe rejected the reading that his refracted narrative methods are meant to mystify readers.
claims.source: Gene Wolfe, interviewed by Larry McCaffery, Science Fiction Studies #46, November 1988
claims.quote: is not to mystify my readers

claims.claim: Wolfe said he drew a floor plan of the house in Free Live Free because he otherwise got tangled in physical questions about the building.
claims.source: Gene Wolfe, interviewed by Larry McCaffery, Science Fiction Studies #46, November 1988
claims.quote: I had to draw a floor plan of

claims.claim: Wolfe listed the kind of physical question the floor plan settled, such as whether the street was visible from a given window.
claims.source: Gene Wolfe, interviewed by Larry McCaffery, Science Fiction Studies #46, November 1988
claims.quote: Could you see the street from this window

claims.claim: Wolfe said he checks that a recurring character is the same person on page 300 as on page 10, and rewrites the earlier page when he prefers the later version.
claims.source: Gene Wolfe, interviewed by Larry McCaffery, Science Fiction Studies #46, November 1988
claims.quote: the same person on page 300 as he was on page 10

claims.claim: Wolfe told Science Fiction Studies that memory is all we have, the present being a knife's edge and the future not existing.
claims.source: Gene Wolfe, interviewed by Larry McCaffery, Science Fiction Studies #46, November 1988

claims.claim: McCaffery credits The Fifth Head of Cerberus with sure control of a variety of imaginative narrative voices.
claims.source: Larry McCaffery, editorial headnote to 'On Encompassing the Entire Universe: An Interview with Gene Wolfe', Science Fiction Studies #46, November 1988
claims.quote: sure control of a variety of imaginative narrative voices

claims.claim: McCaffery characterises the exposition of The Fifth Head of Cerberus as prismatic.
claims.source: Larry McCaffery, editorial headnote, Science Fiction Studies #46, November 1988

claims.claim: Novelist Max Gladstone says Wolfe's readers build interpretations by connecting sentences hundreds of pages apart rather than from anything stated outright.
claims.source: Max Gladstone, 'The Wolfeman', The Third Place (Substack), 2022
claims.quote: building theories by rubbing together two sentences two hundred pages apart

claims.claim: Gladstone says Wolfe's narrators claim eidetic memory and perfect recall and honesty, and then lie or forget.
claims.source: Max Gladstone, 'The Wolfeman', The Third Place (Substack), 2022
claims.quote: They assert their eidetic memories and perfect recall and utter honesty

verdicts.trueWording: "'V.R.T' is told anachronically, with the reader left to piece everything together from a fragmentary, disjointed narrative"
verdicts.note: Raw HTML of ultan.org.uk fetched with a browser UA (HTTP 200) and stripped to text; quote present word for word. Byline confirms 'reviewed by Robert Borski', posted 28 August 2001. The review also names 'V.R.T.' as 'the closing' novella, so 'third novella' holds. Borski writes 'piece everything together' rather than 'the case', though the same review describes the frame as an officer 'seeking to adjudicate the case of John V. Marsch'.

verdicts.trueWording: "I do a minimum of three 'writes' for everything I do-an original and then at least two rewrites"
verdicts.note: Wayback raw capture (id_ URL, HTTP 200) of the DePauw SFS #46 page; header confirms 'Larry McCaffery -- On Encompassing the Entire Universe: An Interview with Gene Wolfe', Science Fiction Studies #46 = Volume 15, Part 3 = November 1988. Quote verbatim in Wolfe's answer on revision.

verdicts.trueWording: "A lot of stuff goes through four drafts, and some of it goes 15 or even more drafts"
verdicts.note: Same raw SFS capture; quote verbatim, immediately after the three-writes sentence. 'some of his work' matches 'some of it'.

verdicts.trueWording: "when I started 'The Fifth Head of Cerberus' I completely rewrote those opening pages at least eight or ten times"
verdicts.note: Same raw SFS capture; quote verbatim. On the page the title is in quotation marks, i.e. Wolfe is naming the novella; the claim's 'The Fifth Head of Cerberus' reads the same either way.

verdicts.trueWording: "because it seemed essential to capture that certain flavor ... the feeling of stagnation which affects a lot of what's to follow"
verdicts.note: Same raw SFS capture; quote verbatim and the causal limb ('because it seemed essential to capture...') is explicit. Wording nuance, not an unsupported limb: Wolfe says the stagnation 'affects a lot of what's to follow', slightly weaker in force and scope than the claim's 'governs what follows'.

verdicts.trueWording: "that's important, especially when I'm trying to capture a specific atmosphere or cultural attitude in a story"
verdicts.note: Same raw SFS capture; quote verbatim. Wolfe's 'especially when' carries the claim's 'matters most when'; he is comparing occasions, and the page separately says character is the element he is most interested in overall.

verdicts.trueWording: "my intent in using these approaches is not to mystify my readers"
verdicts.note: Same raw SFS capture; quote verbatim. The antecedent 'these approaches' is McCaffery's question about Wolfe's 'refracted' methods (memory, dream, unreliable narrators, stories within stories, different points of view), so the 'refracted narrative methods' limb is supported by the page itself.

verdicts.trueWording: "I had to draw a floor plan of the two storys of the house because otherwise I found myself getting tangled up in such details"
verdicts.note: Same raw SFS capture; quote verbatim, and the page names the book as Free Live Free with the action set in 'an old brick house on a city street'. 'Storys' is the page's own spelling.

verdicts.trueWording: "such details as: Could you see the street from this window? Could you see from this room to that room?"
verdicts.note: Same raw SFS capture; quote verbatim as the first of three listed questions (the third is whether Ben Free could hear steps overhead).

verdicts.trueWording: "I want to make sure he's the same person on page 300 as he was on page 10"
verdicts.note: Same raw SFS capture; quote verbatim, of the recurring character Malrubius 'who shows up in widely separated places'. Second limb explicit: 'sometimes I like the man on page 300 better ... so then I have to go back and re write page 10 to make him match the way he appears later on.'

verdicts.trueWording: "Memory is all we have. The present is a knife's edge, and the future doesn't really exist"
verdicts.note: Same raw SFS capture; quote verbatim and both trailing limbs appear in the same two sentences of Wolfe's answer on memory.

verdicts.trueWording: "its sure control of a variety of imaginative narrative voices"
verdicts.note: Same raw SFS capture; quote verbatim in the introductory headnote, whose subject is The Fifth Head of Cerberus ('Cerberus established Wolfe as an eccentric but important new figure in SF. Its prismatic manner of exposition, its sure control...'). The headnote sits inside the piece bylined Larry McCaffery, above the first 'LM:' question, so the attribution holds.
Same raw SFS capture; quote verbatim in the same McCaffery headnote sentence, with 'Its' referring to The Fifth Head of Cerberus.

verdicts.trueWording: "building theories by rubbing together two sentences two hundred pages apart"
verdicts.note: Raw substack HTML fetched with a browser UA (HTTP 200), full post text present, not truncated by a paywall; byline 'Max Gladstone', dated Oct 14, 2022. Quote verbatim. 'rather than from anything stated outright' is supported in substance by the same essay ('vast churning implications invisible to the casual reader'), though not in those words. The quote sits in the paragraph beginning 'Second, when one puts forth a theory' (5th body paragraph, not 4th).

verdicts.trueWording: "They assert their eidetic memories and perfect recall and utter honesty, and then straight-up lie, or forget things"
verdicts.note: Same raw Substack fetch; quote verbatim and the lying/forgetting limb continues the same sentence (which adds 'or have their memories edited out from under them').
